Purity and Formulations.intro: In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or compound. Formulations are mixtures carefully designed for specific purposes.
Purity and Formulations.mnemonic: Pure = ONE thing only, SHARP melting point. Impure = mixture, LOWER and BROADER melting range. Think: a pure diamond is sharp and precise; an impure one is blurry and lower quality!

sections.title: Pure Substances
sections.text: In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one type of element or compound. This is different from the everyday meaning of 'pure'.
points: Contains only one type of particle — one element or one compound; no other substances mixed in
Sharp, precise melting point — changes state at an exact temperature; this is used to test purity
Sharp, precise boiling point — similarly, boils at a specific temperature
Impurities lower the melting point — and broaden the melting range (melts over a range of temperatures instead of at one exact point)
Melting point test — compare to known value; if it matches and is sharp = pure; if lower and broad = impure
Everyday vs chemical 'pure' — 'pure orange juice' means unprocessed; in chemistry 'pure' means one substance only

sections.title: Formulations
sections.text: Formulations are carefully designed mixtures where each component has a specific purpose and the proportions are precisely controlled.
points: Definition — a mixture with precisely controlled proportions designed for a specific use
Each component has a function — e.g. in a tablet: active drug + filler + binder + coating
Medicine — precise drug dose (active ingredient) mixed with excipients; right amount to right place
Fuels — additives improve performance, prevent engine knock, reduce emissions
Cleaning products — surfactants, solvents, enzymes, fragrances in precise amounts
Other examples — alloys, paints (pigment, binder, solvent), fertilisers, cosmetics, foods

sections.title: Testing Purity
sections.text: Melting point and boiling point measurements are the standard experimental methods to assess the purity of a substance.
points: Melting point apparatus — capillary tube with sample; heat slowly; note temperature at which melting begins and ends
Pure substance — begins and ends melting at the same temperature (sharp melting point)
Impure substance — begins melting at a lower temperature than expected; melts over a range of several degrees
Compare to data book — look up the known melting point; a match (and sharpness) confirms purity
Boiling point equally useful — impurities raise the boiling point; pure water boils at exactly 100°C
Chromatography — also used; a single spot in all solvents suggests a pure substance

keyTerms.def: A substance containing only one type of element or compound; has a precise, sharp melting and boiling point
A mixture designed with precisely controlled proportions, where each component serves a specific purpose
The temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid; a sharp melting point indicates purity
A substance present as a contaminant; lowers and broadens the melting point of the main substance
The component of a formulation that provides the intended effect; e.g. the drug in a tablet
An inactive ingredient in a pharmaceutical formulation that aids delivery, stability, or taste

examTips: Pure substance = sharp, precise melting point at the correct literature value. Impure = melts at a lower temperature AND over a range. Always mention BOTH effects of impurities.

Formulations are NOT pure — they are deliberately designed mixtures. The question may ask you to explain why a product is a formulation: answer by saying it is a mixture with specific components in precise proportions.
Impurities LOWER the melting point and RAISE the boiling point. This is the opposite of what students sometimes expect.
commonMistakes: Saying pure water is a formulation — pure water is a pure compound (only H₂O); a formulation is a designed mixture.
Forgetting that impurities LOWER (not raise) the melting point AND broaden the melting range.
Confusing the everyday meaning of 'pure' (natural, unprocessed) with the chemical meaning (contains only one substance).
clozePassages: A pure substance contains only one element or compound. Pure substances have fixed, sharp melting and boiling points. Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point of a substance. These changes in melting and boiling points can be used to detect impurities and assess purity. In everyday language, 'pure' often means natural or unprocessed, but in chemistry it has a precise meaning.

A formulation is a mixture that has been designed to have specific useful properties. Formulations are made by mixing components in carefully controlled proportions. Examples include medicines (where the active ingredient is mixed with excipients), paints (pigment, solvent, binder), alloys, cleaning products, and fuels. The components of a formulation each have a specific function, and the overall properties depend on the precise amounts used.

Pharmaceutical drugs are formulated as tablets, capsules, or liquids. The active ingredient must be delivered in the right amount to the right place. Excipients are inactive ingredients that help the drug remain stable, improve taste, or control release rate. Fertilisers are formulated to contain the right balance of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. The science of formulations is important in food technology, cosmetics, and agricultural chemistry.

Chromatography.intro: Chromatography separates mixtures based on how strongly each component interacts with the stationary and mobile phases. It is used to identify substances.
Chromatography.mnemonic: Rf = distance by Substance ÷ distance by Solvent. Remember: 'Runners (substance) never beat the Starter (solvent front)' — Rf is always less than 1. More soluble = runs further = higher Rf.

sections.title: How Chromatography Works
sections.text: Chromatography separates mixtures because each component distributes differently between the mobile phase (solvent) and stationary phase (paper), causing different rates of movement.
points: Mobile phase — the solvent; moves through or over the stationary phase, carrying dissolved substances
Stationary phase — the paper (or other medium); does not move
Separation principle — substances travel at different speeds based on their solubility in solvent and attraction to paper
More soluble in solvent / less attracted to paper → travels further up; higher Rf value
Less soluble / more attracted to paper → travels shorter distance; lower Rf value
Baseline — drawn in PENCIL below the solvent level; spot placed on baseline before solvent is added

sections.title: Rf Values
sections.text: The Rf value is a ratio that identifies substances — it is constant for a given substance in a given solvent under controlled conditions.
points: Formula — Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front
Always between 0 and 1 — substance can never travel further than the solvent front
Measured from the baseline — both distances measured from where the spot was originally placed
Worked example — substance travels 4.5 cm; solvent front travels 6.0 cm; Rf = 4.5 ÷ 6.0 = 0.75
Same Rf = possibly same substance — but must test in multiple solvents to confirm identity
Characteristic value — like a fingerprint for a substance in a given solvent

callout.label: Rf Formula
callout.text: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Rf is always between 0 and 1. Same Rf in same solvent = possibly same substance.

sections.title: Interpreting Results
sections.text: Analysing a chromatogram allows you to determine how many substances are in a mixture and identify unknowns by comparing Rf values.
points: One spot — substance may be pure (only one component) OR two substances with the same Rf happened to overlap
Multiple spots — definitely a mixture containing at least that many substances
Compare with known standards — run reference substances alongside unknown; matching Rf suggests same substance
Use multiple solvents — same Rf in several different solvents gives much stronger evidence of identity
Locating agents — colourless substances made visible using UV light or ninhydrin spray
Gas chromatography (GC) — separates volatile mixtures; retention time identifies components; can link to mass spectrometry (GC-MS)

keyTerms.def: The ratio of distance moved by a substance to distance moved by the solvent front; always between 0 and 1
The solvent that moves through the chromatography system, carrying dissolved substances with it
The medium that does not move (e.g. chromatography paper); substances interact with this as they travel
A technique that separates mixtures by distributing components between a mobile phase and a stationary phase
In gas chromatography, the time taken for a component to travel through the column — used to identify substances
A chemical spray or UV light used to make colourless spots on a chromatogram visible

examTips: Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent distance. ALWAYS measure both distances from the BASELINE, not from the top or bottom of the paper.
Rf is the same for a substance in the same solvent under the same conditions — this is what makes it useful for identification.
One spot does NOT prove purity — two substances could have the same Rf. To confirm identity, run in multiple solvents AND compare with known standards.
commonMistakes: Measuring the solvent distance from the top of the paper rather than from the baseline — always measure from the pencil baseline.
Saying one matching Rf value proves identity — you need consistent Rf values in multiple solvents AND comparison with reference standards.
Calculating Rf greater than 1 — this is impossible; if your answer is >1, you have measured from the wrong starting point.
clozePassages: Paper chromatography is used to separate and identify mixtures of coloured substances such as dyes in ink. A spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line at the base of the paper. The paper is placed in a solvent which moves up the paper by capillary action, carrying the components with it. Different components travel different distances depending on their solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper.

The Rf value is used to identify a substance in chromatography. It is calculated as: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front. The Rf value is constant for a given substance under the same conditions. By comparing Rf values to known standards, unknown substances can be identified. Chromatography can separate colourless substances too, using UV light or a locating agent to make spots visible.

Gas chromatography (GC) is used to separate mixtures of volatile substances. The sample is vaporised and carried through a column by an inert gas. Components separate based on their interaction with the stationary phase and their boiling points. Each component exits the column at a characteristic retention time. Gas chromatography can be linked to mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to identify each component, making it very powerful for identifying unknown substances.

Identifying Substances.intro: Chemists use a range of tests to identify unknown elements, ions and compounds. Flame tests and gas tests are the most common examples at GCSE.
Identifying Substances.mnemonic: Flame test colours: 'Little Sodium Keeps Calling Copper' = Li crimson, Na yellow, K lilac, Ca orange-red, Cu green. Gas tests: 'Squeaky Hydrogen, Glowing Oxygen, Cloudy CO₂, Bleached Chlorine' — SGCB!

sections.title: Flame Tests
sections.text: Flame tests identify metal ions by the characteristic colour of light emitted when the metal's electrons are excited by heat.
points: Lithium (Li⁺) — crimson/red flame
Sodium (Na⁺) — intense yellow/orange flame (can mask other colours in mixtures)
Potassium (K⁺) — lilac/pale purple flame
Calcium (Ca²⁺) — orange-red flame
Copper (Cu²⁺) — green/blue-green flame
Method — clean platinum/nichrome wire loop; dip in acid then sample; hold in blue Bunsen flame; observe colour

sections.title: Gas Tests
sections.text: Simple chemical tests identify common laboratory gases using a splint, limewater, or damp litmus paper.
points: Hydrogen (H₂) — hold lit splint at mouth of tube → 'squeaky pop' as H₂ ignites
Oxygen (O₂) — hold glowing splint at mouth of tube → splint relights (supports combustion)
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — bubble through limewater (Ca(OH)₂ solution) → turns cloudy/milky white
Chlorine (Cl₂) — hold damp litmus paper at mouth of tube → turns white (bleaches the dye)
Ammonia (NH₃) — hold damp red litmus paper near gas → turns blue (alkaline gas)
Water vapour — blue cobalt chloride paper → turns pink; anhydrous white CuSO₄ → turns blue

sections.title: Ion Tests
sections.text: Precipitation reactions and acid tests identify specific ions in solution by producing characteristic colour changes or precipitates.
points: Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) — add dilute acid → fizzes (CO₂ produced); test gas with limewater to confirm
Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) — add dilute HCl (to remove carbonates first), THEN add BaCl₂ → white precipitate (BaSO₄)
Chloride (Cl⁻) — add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ → white precipitate (AgCl)
Bromide (Br⁻) — add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ → cream precipitate (AgBr)
Iodide (I⁻) — add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ → yellow precipitate (AgI)
Metal ions with NaOH — Cu²⁺ blue precipitate; Fe²⁺ green precipitate; Fe³⁺ red-brown precipitate; Al³⁺ white (dissolves in excess NaOH)

keyTerms.def: A test to identify metal ions by the colour produced when the metal compound is held in a hot flame
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions are mixed together
Calcium hydroxide solution — turns cloudy (milky white) in the presence of carbon dioxide
An analytical technique that identifies elements from the specific wavelengths of light they emit — more precise than flame tests
Adding acidified silver nitrate solution to test for halide ions: white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), yellow (I⁻) precipitate
Adding acidified barium chloride to test for sulfate ions — a white precipitate of barium sulfate forms

examTips: Sodium flame is very intense yellow — it can mask the colours of other metal ions if both are present in a mixture. Mention this limitation.
Gas tests: Oxygen = glowing splint RELIGHTS. Hydrogen = lit splint SQUEAKY POP. These are different tests — do not mix them up.
For the sulfate test: ALWAYS add dilute HCl FIRST to remove any carbonate ions, THEN add BaCl₂. Without this step, a false positive from BaCO₃ is possible.
When describing precipitation reactions in answers: state what you add, what you observe, and what the precipitate is.
commonMistakes: Confusing hydrogen (squeaky pop with LIT splint) with oxygen (relights GLOWING splint) — remember: H is loud (pop), O is glowing.
Saying calcium gives a yellow flame — SODIUM is yellow/orange; calcium is orange-RED. They are different colours.
Forgetting to acidify with HCl before the sulfate test — without this, the precipitate could be barium carbonate (a false positive) rather than barium sulfate.
clozePassages: Flame tests can identify metal ions by the colour they produce when burned. Lithium gives a crimson flame, sodium gives yellow, potassium gives lilac, calcium gives orange-red, and barium gives green. The flame test is quick but not suitable for identifying mixtures. More precise identification uses atomic emission spectroscopy, which can detect very small amounts of elements and identify them from their emission spectra.

Precipitation reactions are used to identify anions and cations. Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution containing metal ions produces a coloured precipitate: copper(II) gives a blue precipitate, iron(II) gives a green precipitate, and iron(III) gives a red-brown precipitate. Adding dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution tests for halide ions: chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide gives a cream precipitate, iodide gives a yellow precipitate.

The presence of carbonate ions can be tested by adding dilute acid — if carbonate is present, carbon dioxide is produced, which turns limewater milky. Sulphate ions are detected by adding barium chloride solution — a white barium sulphate precipitate forms. These chemical tests allow individual ions to be identified in unknown samples. Combined with other analytical techniques, they allow the complete composition of a sample to be determined.
